newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Ayala Corp's latest.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Ayala Corp's latest.

text.p: Ayala Corp of the Philippines launched its latest in the form of a five-year floating rate note issue on Friday.
Asian debt markets were otherwise quiet.

Ayala Corp unit AC International Finance Ltd launched the US$75 million note via arranger BT Asia. The deal pays a margin of 90 basis points over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate and, with fees, an all-in return of 105 basis points.

In May, Ayala brought its debut Eurobond through lead manager JP Morgan, a 5.5-year 8.125 percent bond that was priced to yield 173 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries or roughly 148-150 basis points over LIBOR on a swap basis.

That spread tightened to the mid-150s over Treasuries in the wave of good feeling toward Philippines credits that accompanied the country's Brady exchange, in which collateralized Brady bonds were swapped for uncollateralized sovereign debt.
Traders said the Ayala bond now is trading at Treasuries plus 156 to 167 basis points, or about 130-140 basis points on an after-swap basis.
"It's definately tighter than the Eurobond, but I would expect to see pricing on Philippine paper tighten even more," said one syndicate manager.
The trend toward thinner margins is likely to continue because of the Philippines' growing economy and its generally better outlook, he said.
Philippine bank FRNs have put in a lacklustre performance in the secondary market due to oversupply and ever-tighter prices, but traders said the rarer corporate bonds have fared better.
But some bankers, while acknowledging the Philippines' successes, said the Ayala bond may not be an easy sell because of the tighter pricing.
"Investors would be better off buying the Eurobond in the secondary market," remarked one trader.
Chinatrust Commercial Bank, Credit Lyonnais, Development Bank of Singapore and IBJ Asia are co-arrangers in the FRN.
The inclusion of Chinatrust in the group virtually assures that a significant share of the issue will place with Taiwan banks, bankers said.
Chinatrust joined Bankers Trust as one of the lead managers in a five-year floating rate note for the Philippines' Metrobank back in August.
The deal was the first five-year FRN for a Philippine bank and syndicate managers expressed doubts that the deal would be successful. Previously, three-year tenors were the norm.
In the end, the Metrobank FRN was doubled to US$100 million after a slew of Taiwan banks joined the deal.
Bankers noted that Taiwan banks enjoy a lower cost of funds than their counterparts in South Korea and Japan, for example, so they are more keen to take Philippine paper.
In other news, Korea Development Bank's US$500 million global bond received an enthusiastic response, according to joint lead manager JP Morgan Securities.

"The reason this deal did so well is that since Korea has been invited to join the OECD, a number of new investors have been willing to buy these bonds," said John Massad, head of debt syndication at JP Morgan Securities in New York.
The seven-year bond priced last night to yield 49 basis points over comparable Treasuries, right in the center of its 48-50 basis point indicated range.
